utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take today's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, all. I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Registrar -- sorry. The Usher may escort the witness back to the stand if there is nothing --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As the witness is coming in, Your Honour, I just wanted to indicate -- to request your attention to a matter regarding Ewa Tabeau. She's a Prosecution witness we hope to call as the last witness before the break, and there's matters pending that -- that we need a decision from you about whether we can use her new report, whether she will testify as an expert, et cetera. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks for the reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Markovic. Before Mr. Cvijetic resumes his cross-examination, I would remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Markovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, we can't away from this. We have to keep on going.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I am here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I showed you minutes from a government session of the Republika Srpska of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of 28 July 1992, and we saw that the government discussed and supported the agreement on the conditions and manner of prisoner exchanges. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the 22nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following that, I showed you a -- an agreement that I thought was the relevant one, agreement that was signed in Geneva on the 23rd of May, 1992, and agreed upon by representatives of the Serbian and the Muslim parties, or sides. However, you pointed out that this could not have been the relevant agreement and that the government probably, at its session, discussed and deliberated on another agreement, and I did not show it to you yesterday because I misplaced it; it was in the Prosecutor's binder yesterday and I couldn't pull it out immediately so I would like to do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please pull up P1318.26.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, before you read this first agreement that we have on the monitors, let me just say that the agreement that we are going to discuss is attached to this -- to this contract. Would you please take a look at this contract before I put several questions to you. Have you seen -- have you read through it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You see, this is a contract reached, concluded between two representatives of two commissions, the Serbian commission and the Muslim commission, but with the mediation of UNPROFOR representatives. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, if we look at the text of this agreement, would you agree with me that this was agreement that actually related to one particular exchange, an ad hoc, as it were, exchange, in a certain area, because the agreement does not include some general -- general provisions on the principles which would be applied throughout the territory, the demarcation territory and so on. So let me ask you: Do you know anything about this agreement and can you shed some light on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This agreement, I've never actually seen it before. It is true that it pertains to one particular exchange, a single exchange, and it's probably an exchange somewhere around Ilidza. I assume that, because the Serbian side, the representative whose side on their behalf was Nenad Vanovac, and the stamp was not the commission stamp but, rather, the Serbian Democratic Party of Ilidza stamp, as you can read for yourself, the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party at Ilidza. So probably the agreement and the list relate to the exchange in Ilidza, around Ilidza, or somewhere in that general area. And for this document, itself, I have never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to admit that I've actually -- I did not note what you've just told us about the stamp, but you did confirm that this was a specific exchange that this document relates to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Because we see that the stamp reads Ilidza or -- or Vojkovici, some of those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, do you agree that this issue, the issue of prisoner exchanges in wartime, the free movement of civilians and security of those individuals who are waiting to be exchanged, would you agree that this is a major issue that has to be discussed and decided upon by the highest representatives of the Serbian or Muslim nations specifically, but that the international community should also participate in that type of agreement to provide guarantees that it will be abided by and implemented. Would you agree with what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. Cvijetic, that that was a question and not a speech. I don't know what the witness can make of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, do you consider that this problem that you've also dealt with at the time in question should have been resolved and discussed by the highest authorities and representatives of these parties, as well as members of the international community?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with what you've just said, and especially in relation to the presence of the international community, because whenever I arranged some exchanges, it was always done with the presence of the UNPROFOR because they were there as a sort of judge and referee.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is the following page of the document, and we should have the attachment to the agreement here, and this is something that we would need to discuss now. Mr. Markovic, I'm going give you some time again just to look at the document and then we will comment on it. Have you had the opportunity to look at the first page of the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can see in the introductory paragraph, the agreement is an agreement that is concluded between the highest representatives of the Serbian and the Muslim people, between, thus, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, on behalf of the Republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina and Alija Izetbegovic and representatives of state commissions for the exchange of prisoners, as it says at the top. You will see, however, that the date is missing, so we will remember this bit because when we finish this document -- with this document, I will go back to discuss the point why there is no date here. So let us just go through some of the provisions of this agreement now. You can see in item 1, that the subject of the agreement is noted. This is something that you dealt with in your commission as well. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In item 2, it is said that the exchanges should be carried out through the commissions that should be formed by both sides. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, the priorities are set about the unconditional release of certain categories of persons, and what is meant here are primarily civilians. Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, it is stated that the commissions should exchange the lists of detained persons. And then towards the end, the principle all for all that you mentioned is also referred to. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And just help us here with this principle. If you can just confirm that this principle is supposed to guarantee that there will be no individual trading and bargaining one for one and so on and so forth but it will be an all-for-all exchange. I think you were explaining a little bit about that yesterday. Is that how matters were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that this principle all for all functioned sometime at the very beginning of the war. However, afterwards, the principle was not applied. For example, a high-ranking officer of the Serbian army would be exchanged for 15 or 20 Muslim fighters, and they would be requested by name, so the principle actually became meaningless as the combat progressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I asked you. You will agree with me that the principle was put in the agreement with justification. There was a reason to put it in the agreement. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I would. But I'm noting that the principle was applied at the beginning of the war, for a month or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. We already said that. Paragraph 5, you can see here that the agreement provides for the encouragement of agreements at local levels. And I have to remind you, you said that your Central Commission objectively could not cover the whole territory, and you will agree that this agreement actually acknowledges that. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree completely. Because physically it was impossible for us to approach and to cover everything, because of the roads and everything. However, the commissions were unable to provide us with the lists of exchanged persons also because it was not possible to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Item 6, we can just briefly say that the agreement is also covering the exchange of dead bodies. So it is not only about the exchange of people who are alive but also the exchange of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to paragraph 7, which is on the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, there is an agreement on the release of all detained JNA soldiers. Do you see that? And then item 8 refers to other priority categories, and these would be journalists, medical science and culture workers, public workers, priests, and so on and so forth. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you can see in paragraph 9 the agreement is reached on the humane treatment of prisoners. And I think this principle is also noted in the decision on your commission.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only do I remember it; I know it off by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What is interesting to me is paragraph 11, where the agreement provides for the sides enabling each other to check on the living conditions of the prisoners, guaranteeing mutual safety and return. So let us try to interpret this as meaning that you as a representative of the commission and your colleague, on the Muslim side, could cross the line of separation wherever you had information that there were prisoners and you had the right to inspect those facilities. Do you interpret this provision in the same way, in the way that I have just interpreted it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the agreement reached with the Muslim side that is how it should have been. However, this was not actually possible to implement. Who among the Serbs could enter the notorious Viktor Bubanj prison in the barracks of the same name or enter the central prison which is located in central Sarajevo? So this actually never happened on either side; I have to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The gist of my questions relating to this agreement actually is aimed at establishing the reasons why this did not happen. So now we will quickly move to item 14 where the parties would commit themselves to prevent occurrences of unlawful arrests, to ban blackmail, and I think that we will agree that this principle all for all would eliminate these options from item 14. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a large degree. Yes, of course, I agree entirely. And the principle all for all has been eliminated here completely and I will explain that with one detail. For example, when a brother of one of the Serbs would be arrested, then the army would arrest a Muslim, and then there would be private negotiations for the exchange of his brother for this Muslim person. There were many such occurrences because war is a difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see item 17 of the document; also in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you can see here that the contracting parties have committed themselves to invite representatives of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees and UNPROFOR representatives as well as representatives of the Red Cross of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Red Cross of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and representatives of the International Red Cross. We have now come to the introductory part of my question. You would agree, wouldn't you, that an agreement as detailed as this could be applied only with the presence of all these entities referred to in paragraph 17. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, absolutely. It's an ideally written agreement except that it was not possible to implement it in the field. And I'm noting here that the agreement was signed only by the Serbian side. It was signed by the president of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and the president of the exchange commission, Nenad Vanovac. And there are no signatures by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Filip Vukovic. So I'm not sure to what extent this agreement is valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My reasons for dealing with this agreement precisely are in this, and that is that it was evidently not signed by the Muslim side because we will remind ourselves again of the introductory party where there was no date because it was to be expected that they would sign such agreement. So there was just a draft agreement, or an offer, from the Serbian side to the Muslim side to resolve this particular problem in this particular way. Would you agree with what I have just said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. And evidently, the Muslim side did not agree to it because they probably didn't like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that by signing and implementing this agreement, many ugly things that later happened in the area of prisoner exchanges and prisoner camps would have been prevented had both sides bilaterally respected each one of these provisions and had the international community guaranteed the implementation of this agreement. Would not those negative things that happened have been prevented by that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the agreement had been implemented, it would have been very good for both sides and all the ugly things could have been avoided, especially if members of SFOR had always been present during prisoner exchanges, or members -- representatives of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you said just a short while ago that you thought that the reason why the Muslims hadn't signed this draft agreement was that they probably didn't like it. What makes you conclude that they didn't like it? What, in your view, would have caused the Muslims to abstain from signing, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know precisely, but I believe that this agreement did not go in their favour for the simple reason that only in the city of Sarajevo, where I live, there were more than 200.000 Serbs left behind, and pursuant to this agreement, they should have released them all, freed them from Sarajevo. But they held them as hostages and mistreated them in their prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the Muslim side held 200.000 Serbs in prisons in -- within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in prisons but in Sarajevo itself and some in prisons. Because people were living in Sarajevo but under daily stress, fear, daily killings in buildings, but they were unable to leave Sarajevo in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did the -- did the draft agreement make any distinction between prisoners of war and detained civilians? Forgive me for not picking this up when we went through the agreement, but I didn't see any provision to this effect so I'm just asking you, who are more familiar with the draft, if -- if any such distinction was made in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. I worked in the Commission for Exchanges of Prisoners of War, and I could not exchange them. However, the citizens of Serb ethnicity who lived in Sarajevo, I could not use them for these exchanges because they did not consider them prisoners. They considered them and used them as shields, human shields, during the combat operations around Sarajevo. Therefore, they did not have an opportunity to leave Sarajevo either through the commission or any other way. The only thing that I could do is exchange prisoners of war but not regular citizens and civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, I thought you told us yesterday that you only dealt with the exchange of civilians; whereas, exchange of prisoners of war would be left to the military commissions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of my commission was the Commission for an Exchange of Prisoners of War. But we also exchanged civilians. Let me explain it. Prisoners of war were civilians. They would, for instance, capture 100 Serbs in Sarajevo and then bring them to the demarcation line and they were considered, in that case, prisoners of war. As for the military aspect, members of both parties would exchange members of the armies, of the respective armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But it seems to me, from what you now tell us, that both parties, actually, seemed to completely ignore the definitions of a prisoner of war, according to the Geneva Convention, the Third Convention. Was that done deliberately, or was it just by ignorance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my view, it was out of ignorance. In my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, yes, because if you were to abide by the Geneva Conventions - this goes for both parties to the conflict - then the detention of civilians would be unlawful unless you would detain them for some -- for the purpose of criminal investigation of some sort. But just to detain civilians in great numbers would be in contravention of the -- both the Third and the Fourth Convention. So my question is: If there was any awareness about these matters in the commission that you worked in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, of course, there was a certain awareness, and we tried to abide and comply as much as we could to the Geneva Conventions' provisions. However, Judge, you must understand that this was a war of major proportions, and I don't know what your opinion is on this, but do you think that the American army in Vietnam or in Iraq applied those principles? As for us, we did have to -- and, of course, they would have had to abide by the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. I mentioned this just for comparative reasons, for comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have no doubts that the rules are broken in every war that has ever been fought in history. But, you see, I'm a Judge and my job to actually make sure that these international norms are respected. Because if they weren't, then things could get really out of hand. Back to you, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Mr. Markovic, this draft agreement we are talking about now did you know of it at the time, or did you learn it lately here or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've seen it for the first time here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So when you answered Mr. Cvijetic saying that you agreed that evidentially the Muslim side did not agree to it because they probably didn't like it, that is not something that you know of but that's something you are deducting from the fact that there is no signature on the Muslim side; is that right? You didn't know that this was just a draft and not a signed agreement, or did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't know. I used the word "I assume." That they didn't sign it because it didn't suit them precisely because of the Serbs who were in Sarajevo, held captive there practically, and they couldn't leave the town. They were used as human shields to dig trenches around Sarajevo and for other physical labour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But you don't know if it has ever been signed or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I can see that it wasn't, here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would just like to clarify this by putting a few questions. Had this agreement been signed, you would have been the first, as a member of the commission, to know that there was such agreement in place because you would, among other things, have to apply their provisions; correct? Its provisions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could know about it only if Mr. Vanovac, who is the undersigned person here, sent it to me. That would have been the only way for me to have any knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I would just like to remind you of a question that the Prosecutor asked yesterday. In one of the documents, the president of the commission on the Bosnian side, Filip Vukovic, regarding the free flow of civilians that is also mentioned here, referred to it as ethnic cleansing. In that respect, in order to clarify this for the Trial Chamber -- or, rather to provide an illustration, we should mention what the scale of the flow of civilians was and the problems that this posed to the authorities. I would now just like to mention a few facts that I assume you are familiar with. You said that you live and work in Bijeljina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before the war that town, the centre itself, numbered 35.000 inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around 36.000, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the war and after the war the number of registered inhabitants, new inhabitants was 52.000. They were refugees or displaced persons. Do you know this fact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this fact. Bijeljina numbers today around 135.000 people, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the -- could the witness please repeat the number of refugees who moved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please repeat the figure that you have, because we have the wrong number here. According to you, how many people moved in, subsequently, into Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 100.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know the fact that at least twice as many people stayed or passed through Bijeljina, looking for some other place where they could actually settle and find some kind of shelter and accommodation. Do you know that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to object at this point. This is in the nature of tu quoque. We're not tying it to any specific dates. If it's between 1992 and 2010, there could be all kinds of reasons those people passed through, and without that connection, I don't think this evidence is very relevant or useful to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are discussing generally the problem of refugees and displaced persons, and that is the problem that this witness actually dealt with in his work. And after I mentioned these -- some these facts, I will actually -- this is just to provide the foundation for the question that I will put after this and I will go through this briefly and quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have another objection too. Mr. Cvijetic keeps talking about "these facts I'm suggesting to you." Mr. Cvijetic is not a witness and it's not a fact. He can ask a question based on something he knows but he can't call it a fact at this stage. And he keeps doing it and I would ask that he be directed to stop doing it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Cvijetic, you must both come rapidly to the point that are you trying to make and remember, as Mr. Hannis has cautioned and as I attempted some while ago to point out to you, you're counsel, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I will do my best. If you noticed, my questions were direct. They were not leading questions. I just asked the witness whether he knew the bit of information that I gave him. So now could you just briefly tell us, do you know -- did you know about that last figure that I mentioned, about the people who were there in transit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Because not all people could stay in Bijeljina. They would move on to Serbia, Bratunac, Srebrenica, Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let me ask you this: You will agree, won't you, for Republika Srpska to resolve this problem was to tell these people, You were the victim of ethnic cleansing and just go back to where you have come from. Would this have resolved the problem, according to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it would have resolved the problem, no way. The simple reason being that, for instance, today, only 1 per cent of Sarajevo population are Croats, and some 4 to 5 per cent are Serbs. And to this day, people are leaving Sarajevo for all sorts of reasons, because they can't get a job, because of religious discrimination, and for all sorts of other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In other words, this mass movement of the populations, the one, the second, and the third group, was something that had to be accepted as a result of the war. And you will agree with me that the authorities of Republika Srpska dealt with this problem and did not ignore the fact or the -- the claim that it was in the aftermath of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I object to that question. It is vague. Which mass movements of the population, the one, the second, the third group? When in time is that? Which people is it? From where to where? How does that relate to anything in our case? That needs some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, the agreement that you see before you, was it directed at resolving this problem in the proper way?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object again. It's vague. Which problem? And what does "proper way" mean? It's the problem of prisoners? It's the problem of movement of population? Which problem is being asked about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, simply the problem that is dealt with in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have pointed to us in the agreement what problem is being addressed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- I don't know how helpful this, what we have now gotten bogged down in, is going to be the Trial Chamber at the end of the day. The -- Mr. Cvijetic, you have spent a considerable amount of time setting the background to this situation and eliciting the witness's observations, in light of his own experience. But for our purposes, could we move on to the precise point that you are trying to make as a matter of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the essence is this. As this agreement was not signed and therefore implemented, this problem in Republika Srpska was dealt with in the manner that I showed yesterday, when I showed the witness some documents of the state organs, and I would like now to show how Republika Srpska continued to deal with this problem at the local level because this agreement was -- had not been signed. So the point is -- the point we want to make is that Republika Srpska had to resolve this problem irrespective of the fact there were no signatures of both sides, and the problem could not be resolved bilaterally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before, Mr. Hannis responds, and I expect I know what is he going to say, aren't you sliding into the tu quoque defence. I assume that was the point you were going to make, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That and also, Your Honour, maybe it's just me but I still don't understand what "this problem" is. I'm simply asking him to explain what he is talking about. And he keeps referring to the general term of "this problem." I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the territory of Republika Srpska, and we mentioned one town alone, receives 100.000 people from elsewhere, refugees and displaced persons, then that does pose a problem, that the highest organs of authorities have to deal with in a manner that we point -- showed yesterday and that we will see here, too, and that's a problem that cannot be resolved by shutting your eyes and just claiming that this is the problem to do with ethnic cleansing and we're not going to deal with it. So what I'm trying to show here today, and I've shown it yesterday, I would like to show a few documents to show how Republika Srpska tried to resolve this problem by using various methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I would remind you that the stage of the trial that we're at is that we -- evidence is being led from witnesses. You are in the process of cross-examining this witness, so you are testing and probing the evidence that he has given on behalf of the Prosecution and challenging it. But the question of conclusions and -- and what arguments you would wish to make, you would reserve for the end of the exercise when all of the evidence is in. So if you would confine yourself to getting the evidence from the witness while the witness is on the stand, we could get ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. Can we now show the witness document P60.8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, can you see the title of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the first page of the document, please. And there is an affirmation by the translator; I just wanted to note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you can see here that the problem of the refugee population in the area of Sanski Most, for example, is something that the municipal civilian protection staff was dealing with. And you said that some parts of the Serbian Republic of the Krajina were inaccessible to members of the commission for certain periods of time. Can you confirm, however, whether this organ that was dealing with this question was one of those authorised to resolve this problem?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday, Mr. Cvijetic, that Crisis Staffs were established in all the municipalities which were practically the Alpha and Omega of the work of the municipality. This municipality of Sanski Most I never visited privately and not during the war, so this is an order based on the conclusions of the municipal staff of Sanski Most. But, like I said, I never saw this order before, and I never went to the Sanski Most municipality myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The question was whether the municipal civilian protection staff was supposed to be dealing with this problem. This is what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these were civilians, then, yes, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going move immediately to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D03, please, 4458.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can see here that the care for individuals in the centre in Trnopolje is being dealt along with the participation of the International Red Cross and they're asking for support in food and -- and other supplies. So is this one of the entities that should have been dealing with this question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because, in a way, that's part of the description of the duties of the Red Cross, because what is being requested here is food, flour, meat, and so on, fuel and so on and so forth. So I think that it is proper for the organisation of the Red Cross to be dealing with matters that have to do with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now rounded off - at least I think - of all the key state organs and factors from the Presidency, the government, the army, down to the local organs, which were dealing with the issues of detention facilities, the movement of civilians, and providing assistance and care for the population. Finally, I am going to show you three documents by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit 1D55, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, at the time this order was adopted, you were still a member of the commission so I'm not sure if you actually saw this document or not. But, please, can you now read the contents of the documents? If you're able to; the letters are very small.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, just go ahead, read it and then I'm going to put some questions to you. Have you managed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about the delineation of responsibilities and the authority of the Ministry of the Interior when we're talking about these detention facilities, and you restricted that to facilities that were within the public security stations, which is where the police had the right to detain persons up to three days.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you say that, and now that you see this -- did you say that based on your general knowledge of police affairs and regulations, or did you say that on the basis of the knowledge of this particular document? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was quite specifically formulated and it states that the security of collection centres shall be the direct responsibility of the Serbian army and members of the reserve police can be engaged on these tasks. I know that the minister, in a document of his, issued orders for all reserve police force members to be demobilised from the police and to be made available for the disposition of the Army of Republika Srpska. I read this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you read item 2 of this document to the very end and I think that you will find what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, just read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what it says, what I was referring to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question at the beginning was whether -- do you -- are you aware of the regulations on -- of the Law of Internal Affairs, allowing the police to deal with matters like this only in their own public security stations, and are they able to then keep these persons detained for a maximum of three days? Is that what the regulations state? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Law on Interior Affairs, it specifically says that a person can be detained in a public security facility up to three days, so one, two, and up to a maximum of three days. And this is in police stations which have the adequate facilities for such detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And this order is dealing precisely with those facilities, what they should look like and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the next document? This is 1D56.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your answer was not recorded completely, so ... You can see here Mr. Stanisic's order about the applications of the provisions of international laws of war and adherence to the conventions on the treatment of prisoners of war and so on and so forth. Yesterday, responding to a question from the Prosecutor, you said that policemen, when they're engaged on military assignments, are under the command of the army, and they act pursuant to orders from the army.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. As soon as members of the police are transferred to military units, they are immediately subordinated to the military officers and bound by their orders. They are considered to be soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall that I showed you an order from the commander-in-chief, President Karadzic, ordering that all these international convention regulations be applied?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Stanisic, with this order, orders, in a general way, to the members of the police that if they should find themselves in a situation, even if they are not under the jurisdiction of the MUP but are in the status of soldiers, they should comport themselves pursuant to the regulations as they are stated here. So that applied to you in the same way, regardless of the fact that you were under the jurisdiction of the government and were a member of a government commission. I think you said that -- this was said in a meeting in a conversation. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. But here in the last paragraph it is stated that persons who violate the regulations and act contrary to our legal and international regulations in this field and so on and so forth, regardless of whether they were members of the MUP or the army, it is necessary to immediately start gathering information and documentation and submit criminal reports to the authorised prosecutor's office. Regardless of whether these were soldiers or policemen, if they commit a criminal act, criminal reports have to be submitted to the authorised prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have one more document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D57.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We can see here that the Ministry of Interior, and it says in the second sentence, regardless of its jurisdiction, should act pursuant to the request of the Ministry of Health, Work, and Social Security and assisted in the collection of certain data about these facilities that we spoke about yesterday and today. And it says that this was done at the request of the International Committee of the Red Cross. So the ministry did deal with this problem to the extent that it was able to assist other authorised organs that were authorised to deal with this problem. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Because this refers to data that was gathered by the Ministry of Health, and the minister instructed the centres and the stations of public security to collect the names of the places, who formed or set up those camps, the institutions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going show you one more document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is P731.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We can see that this is a report or action pursuant to a dispatch by the public security station of Rogatica, where the chief of that station reports on the situation in his area, and then, in this second larger paragraph, speaks about the military engagement of members of the public security station and the problems that it encountered. And then at the end of that paragraph, it is said that after a struggle with the military organs, they managed to keep 50 per cent of their force in order to be able to perform their regular duties. Do you see that at the end of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What I am interested in is the problem -- one problem that was encountered and that the chief was forced to resolve in an ad hoc manner, again, regardless of jurisdiction, and this is in the last paragraph but one, if you are able to read it. After the army and certain civilian organs left a group of civilian population out of the zone of combat, he literally says: "Although pursuant to the Law on Internal Affairs they were not under our jurisdiction, we guarded those persons and transferred them to the territory controlled by the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague is drawing my attention to the fact that the break is -- it's time for a break, so perhaps it would be good for the witness to have time to acquaint himself with this document before I can put some questions to him on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- when you say "have time to acquaint himself with the document," you're inviting him to read it during the break or what? I -- I don't follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no objection if a hard copy is provided to him to look at during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, well, that can be done. And we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will be brief, Mr. Markovic. I assume that you've seen the report and read through it. I will only -- yes, we have the second page. Now here we see that the chief of the station is describing why he has done as he has, as described in the document. And what I would like to ask you is this: In the first part, he says that he was not bound by law to take any action. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: He informed about this incident. Now, let's see, if he received this dispatch on the 25th of July, he informed thereof the centre of the security stations in August. Now what I would like to know is whether he informed your commission and whether you knew about this transfer of civilians. Answer with just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this. But the army brought them in, and neither the army authorities nor the civilian authorities wanted to take any responsibility for them so they just transferred their responsibility, as it were, to the police which then had to do something, and they simply let them go. This was a -- an attempt to remove the population, the civilian population, from areas where there was fighting. Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, thank you, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am Defence counsel Igor Pantelic, and I'm the Defence counsel for Mr. Zupljanin. Unfortunately, we didn't have occasion to meet these past days. My colleague spoke with you, but I will continue with the questioning in line with what we've heard before for the Trial Chamber's benefit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My first question is this. Based on information that I have from client and certain exhibits that the Defence has, Mr. Zupljanin never participated in any kind of discussions to do with exchanges of prisoners or populations and so on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, he never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution on 26th of February, 2008, I found, as I read through it, a very tragic and moving incident described therein. And for the Trial Chamber to get a better picture, could you please tell us briefly what this was about. I am referring to the incident where Croatian soldiers from the HVO were supposed to be exchanged for Serbian prisoners of war and the Croatian prisoners of war were detained in the military camp Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you please describe to the Trial Chamber what you witnessed during the exchange and please describe how you felt about it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will begin with my arrival in Banja Luka. When I arrived Banja Luka, on orders from the prime minister, I first went to my own base, as it were. That's the CSB in Banja Luka, where I met Mr. Zupljanin for the first time. We met very briefly, a couple of minutes. I went to see him so that he could tell me and my colleague who was with me, Mr. Slobodan Avlijas, where the Banja Luka court was, and we were looking to meet with the president of the court, Mr. Jovo Rosic, who is unfortunately -- who has unfortunately passed away. Mr. Zupljanin called Mr. Rosic and he said that we had come to arrange this exchange. I met with Mr. Rosic and Mr. Branko Dokic, who was the dean of the electrical engineering school in Banja Luka at the time, and they were representatives in the commission of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. That's what it was called at the time. I had lists with me of Croatian prisoners that were being sought by the Croatian side because I received them by fax from a certain Mario Plejic, who lived in Dusseldorf, somewhere in Germany anyway, and we exchanged fax messages and lists in that manner. I confirmed that I had found all these men and that all the men that they were asking, that were on the list, will be -- would be exchanged. Mr. Rosic Avlijas, myself, and Dokic went to Manjaca where we took over, took with us a certain number of prisoners of war of Croatian ethnicity who had been captured during combat. From there, we boarded buses, two or three buses, I can't recall exactly, and went to Knin. When we arrived in Knin it was already dark so we spent the night there, and the Croatians who were on the buses were guarded by the Army of the Knin Krajina. The next day we left in a convoy of buses for a place called Zitnic, which was in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. There, we met members of the Croatian commission, Mr. Ivan Bender, Valentin Coric, and two other men that I didn't know. In these negotiations, a member of the international mission also was present. I think his name was Martin --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- from Portugal. After some discussion and negotiation they asked to board the buses and check whether the men that they had sought were on the buses. We, on our part, had brought every single man that they had requested. And then, from there on, we continued to another place called Pakovo Selo, near Sibenik, where we were supposed to check our list of our people that we had sought and that had been agreed with Mr. Plejic. That's what we thought. When we arrived there, we were surprised, first, when the people started boarding the buses, there were very few men. There were women mostly and even young women with their children, babies. Perhaps 5 per cent of the people that were on the list actually showed up. We didn't know what to do and then Mr. Jovo Rosic, as the president of the court and the most senior member of the commission among us, went back to Zitnic and made a telephone call, probably to the prime minister, Mr. Djeric, and when he returned he said there will be no exchange. Of course, the Croats began protesting, because, you know, for our people -- for our people it wasn't really simple. They were almost free and now they were supposed to go back to hell. I'm sure they didn't enjoy it there. Now, these -- this was a very difficult situation. There were people crying, the women and children, even some of the Croatian prisoners were crying. After this, on order from the prime minister, we took them back to Manjaca and left them where we had taken them from originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Markovic, let me take you to that year, 1992. There's an impression here, and this is what the Prosecution is trying to build up, that the entire situation and atmosphere was quiet, peaceful, and that everything should follow in an orderly fashion, and every regulation and provision of the law should be applied by. Now, let me ask you this: When -- during the process of establishment of Republika Srpska, there were a lot of organisational and other problems and all authorities, all government organs, local and government -- and at the government level, had a lot of difficulties in organising this in a timely fashion because events just followed one after another at great speed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Other than the documents that we received on how we were to proceed in our work, we also received a document from the mission, international mission, which basically followed the same rules. But have you to understand that in these circumstances, in the chaos of war it was practically impossible to implement all -- and comply with all of these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In answering my colleague Cvijetic's questions, you discussed that and I would now like to set up a framework, a legal framework within which we have to work. Now, do you know that in -- on the 12th of May, 1992, the Assembly of Republika Srpska declared a state of war. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, I was already a member of the commission and I was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As an experienced police officer, you know that in circumstances of an immediate threat of war, the army has -- and the police have certain rules to abide by and they have to be resubordinated to the army.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You've commented a document that Mr. Cvijetic showed you. That's P189. And I would now like quickly to go through it and discuss certain matters therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please pull it up, P189. Here we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Markovic, we see in the preamble to these instructions that it was adopted -- that they were adopted, pursuant to an order from the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of 13 June 1992, and these instructions are being issued by the Ministry of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In item 1, the Ministry of Defence, for all practical purposes, issues an order to members of the MUP as well to comply with certain rules and regulations in keeping with the -- what we've earlier said about the resubordination of the MUP to the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If we look at the paragraph 4 now of these instructions, it says there that the reception centres for captured persons shall be determined by a senior officer with a rank of company commander or higher; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We will not go through all the items, the other items or other articles talk about conditions that should exist in all these centres and reception centres, detention centres and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us move to page 3 of the Serbian or B/C/S version. The last three digits are 451, the last three digits of the ERN number. That's right. We see number 18, please. Can we please have number 18 on the screen in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In item 18 it is stated that for organisation and location of the camps, it is the commanders of the corps of the VRS of the Bosnia and Herzegovina -- it's the responsibility of the corps commanders. So all this was within the systematic regulations that define the role of the army in such conditions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And if you remember, there was an order we've seen yesterday issued by General Ratko Mladic about establishment of camps where it is stated that the VRS should have exclusive control of such camps, that each of the corps has a task to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Markovic, let us look into the circumstances prevailing in the Autonomous Region of Krajina in 1992. So if you have any information about that, I would like to hear your opinion. As far as we know, the entire territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was, practically speaking, a front line that was even encircled by the enemy forces until the corridor was made. They were encircled by the enemy forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us analyse the situation in the area of Prijedor, so-called Potkozarje region, if you have, of course, any information about that. In strong conflicts in that area, the VRS was very active in the period of April until July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to object there. The evidence in this case is that the VRS wasn't created until the middle of May 1992, so the question needs to be reformulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Since my colleague Mr. Hannis insists on being perfectly precise, and this is an objective fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The fighting in the area of Prijedor was between very strong Muslim units and the forces of the Serbian Territorial Defence until May 12th, when the VRS was established, and, as of 12th of May, the fighting was between the VRS and its subordinated units and very strong Muslim forces in the area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Together with the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: These were hard battles with many victims on the Serbian side as well, with a lot of blood spilled.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In course of such fighting, unfortunately, as a consequence of military operations, the civilian population of all three ethnicities was in danger.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then the relevant command of the VRS ordered, in accordance with international law, that civilian population should be protected, and that's why Trnopolje reception centre was established, where civilians could find some kind of shelter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You were referring to Prijedor municipality and then the so-called region but the name of the region is not in the transcript, and I would like to know what region you were talking about where these heavy fighting were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You mentioned it but it isn't on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the purpose of transcript let us repeat. The fighting took place in the area of Prijedor and the region of Potkozarje. This region means, in translation, "surrounding Mount Kozara." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, according to the information that we have, Trnopolje was an open-type reception centre, where civilian population could freely enter or leave at any point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: However, the problem regarding Trnopolje got worse with time, mainly because of the food supply problems and other supply problems, and then the Red Cross from Prijedor also reacted to the situation. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We've seen a document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D9 -- apologies, 1D03-4458.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is the document my learned colleague Cvijetic asked you about. As we see here, the situation on the 12th of September, 1992, was very serious, a shortage of food, fuel for heating, and the municipal Red Cross of Prijedor reacts by sending reports to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Executive Committee, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, although you were not in the area at the time, but you did have information that all such centres faced similar problems because of the war conditions and because it was very hard to organise everything required in relation to feeding the people and so on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If there is no objections -- I don't know if that document was admitted. If there is no objection from my learned friend Mr. Hannis, I would like to -- to tender it, although it was uploaded by our friends from Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do object to it, Your Honour. This witness can't speak to it. He wasn't at Trnopolje. He doesn't know who wrote this document. He doesn't know anything about it. I object to its admission through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe we could MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D93 marked -- this will be Exhibit 2D93, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's marked for identification pending a suitable witness being able to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I was just trying to speed up this process, but, okay, no problem at all. Thank you so much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, please, I suppose your actual line of question goes to the challenge of one or more of 39 adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Can -- may I remember you that you should announce which facts you are challenging that way. If you could, that would be very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you bear with me one second, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If you are not able to do it right now, you can do it perhaps after the next break or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record. Thank you. Thank you so much for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the next document I would like to show to you and to discuss with you is the document that you already talked about. It's 560 from the Prosecutor's 65 ter list. We can see here that the author of the document was the warden of the Trnopolje centre, Mr. Pero Curguz. And on the 8th of October, 1992, he reports again to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor and its Executive Committee about problems in relation to bread, flour and so on. In the end, at the end of the first paragraph, he is saying that there is many people coming in, that there's about 3.500 of them already there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So the problem with Trnopolje is still active at the time. He is then saying that although the centre is officially closed, people keep coming, because people are feeling insecure and feel threatened because of the conflicts of war, and that's the reason why people do go there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document for MFI, please, if it is appropriate. Thank you. Because it is related to previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification, again pending admission through a -- a witness to whom there's a closer nexus.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 2D94, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could only have your answer in the transcript as well. So, my question was: The combat activities in the area was what prompted the influx of people to Trnopolje and the Red Cross is trying to do its best to make arrangements for the people.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the safety of the people was the main thing. They were safe in Trnopolje. There's -- as you can see, there is mention of 50 per cent of children between 1 and 12 years. They were safe in the centre. They did have food and the rest -- well, to some extent at least, they had it, thanks to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at P194. While we're waiting for this document, let me just say it's a report by the commission of the Republika Srpska government consisting of Mr. Vojin Lale, who was Assistant Minister for Justice, and Mr. Erkic, who was an inspector in the MUP. This commission visited the object between the 10th and the 15th of August -- or, rather, facilities in Krajina region; namely, Trnopolje, Omarska, Keraterm, Krings in Sanski Most, and two other centres in Bosanski Samac. Let us deal with Trnopolje and the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the following page of this document put up on the screen. Or, rather, the third page. So one more page, please. The last three ERN numbers are 062. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, it is stated that this settlement of Trnopolje is under the protection of the VRS and that one can see in Serbian and English a sign saying "open reception centre". Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, the commission writes, that certain problems persist in relation to provision of food but that the local Red Cross organisation and a Muslim organisation called Merhamet are doing all they can to improve the conditions. And then, on the following page of this report, the commission --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The commission states or writes about the conditions in the POW detention centre called Omarska. They discuss the conditions found there, and then explains what conditions were like in Keraterm, Sanski Most and Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we please move to page 5 of the document. The last three ERN numbers are 066. So, conclusions or concluding remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, it is a known fact that on the basis of the reaction by the Assembly of Republika Srpska in July, but also in August of 1992, such centres were subjected to intensive control and also that because of international outcry in relation to these centres. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In item 1, the commission criticises the government of Republika Srpska and says that the government did not pay appropriate attention to the problems relating to these facilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then in the following items, the commission speaks about inadequate conditions, as well as noting that the government should have, through the Ministry of Defence, have taken appropriate measures; is that correct? This is in paragraph marked 3. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then, on the next page in the B/C/S - that is, paragraph 5 - attention is drawn to the lack of suitable regulations regarding the treatment of civilian refugees which is particularly evident in the case of Trnopolje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we could draw a conclusion on the basis of all this, on the basis of the circumstances and facts here, that there was quite a lot of disorganisation and lack of direction and lack of correct interpretation of the regulations and standards that had led to a number of abuses even, in this area, by a number of individuals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: However, the government and the defence ministry are those in charge of taking measures and taking the lead on this and not the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because the police, within the constitutional system, is actually an organ of state administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And we can see on this page, especially in paragraph marked 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That certain measures are being proposed by the commission to the government as to what the government should do on this matter. But what is important to me at this time is that when we look at item 5 that speaks about Trnopolje and possible manipulation of the public media and public opinion, I have a specific question. We know that representatives of foreign media did tour those places and we know that members of the foreign media exaggerated and presented the circumstances there unrealistically. I think you started to explain this but were interrupted by the Prosecutor. Do you have any information about Trnopolje or anything in terms of media manipulation and public manipulation regards conditions in Trnopolje? You wanted to say something but were interrupted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps one of the key things is that scene when that tall, thin, young man, with his bones practically protruding, is standing behind barbed wire fence. And when the journalist shows only that sequence, when you can only see him and the barbed wire fence, but actually there were shovels and other tools, working tools, standing behind that fence, and she used that opportunity to make that photograph and that photograph was broadcast all over the world. And everything was presented in a very negative way. People were presented as criminals, as inhumane, even though that is very far from the truth, far from the truth of what the photograph is showing. And broader than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war years, you had witnessed a high degree of manipulation by the foreign media, in terms of the events and objective reporting from the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to say that after the war, as inspector in the police administration of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, I went to Prijedor to inspect the work of that public security station -- actually Prijedor was a public security centre at the time, and I did go to Trnopolje. Of course, the war was over, and that's when people explained to me what kind of a camp it was. My colleagues who were there explained to me. We toured Trnopolje. They explained what was being done in that camp, that that photograph that was shown had no relation to the truth, that actually only 2 metres away from there was a barbed wire fence behind which a -- a wire fence behind which tools were stored, but it was really contrived to make it seem as if it was some -- Auschwitz practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, 45, 4, page 45, line 4, I believe the witness says that the -- the wire length was 2 metres only. That was my understanding. Maybe this can be checked with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: A small correction to the transcript. Can you please confirm what my colleague has just said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was two, two and a half metres, an enclosure where tools were kept, and this was set apart to prevent them perhaps from fighting or injuring each other in a fight. I mean, this is what my colleagues told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now about the functioning of the police and about information from this topic. It's important that we cover that topic, and we would need to look at a certain number of documents in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we look at document, Exhibit 1D57. This is a Stanisic Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course, I'm not going to ask you to confirm if you have seen those documents or not, but I'm just using them as a certain illustration of the methods of work of the Ministry of the Interior. So I have a few questions on that topic. Here in this exhibit we can see a dispatch sent on the 24th of August, 1992, from the Ministry of the Interior to all Security Service Centres and public security stations, where MUP, on the basis of the request of the ministry, is requesting certain information regarding the camps, the dates when they were set up, who ordered these persons to be brought in, and a deadline is given until the 30th of August, 1992, for the MUP to inform about this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course, you, as an experienced policeman, police professional, will confirm that when the Ministry of the Interior orders something like this and because of its urgency, we can see that the dispatch was sent both to the centres and to the public security stations individually too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this was upon the request of the Ministry of Health, Work, and Social Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Precisely. And now let's look at the next document related to this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is 65 ter document 536. It's Prosecution Exhibit P972, in fact, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
